patches.fact: Descent line
patches.expect: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the class 3–4 blocky terrain back down the rising traverse to the step above Crystal Pass. Route-specific rappel counts for this exact Crystal Pass/NE line are thinly documented, but the Constance massif's upper terrain that Inner Constance shares with its neighbor — broken, gendarmed ridge steps on notoriously poor rock — is commonly down-climbed by confident parties with one short rappel used through the single steepest step near the top by those who prefer it. Plan on roughly one rappel of about 30 m/100 ft; a single 30 m rope (or a 60 m doubled) is enough length. Treat any anchor as natural rather than fixed: the only documented technical route on this peak explicitly notes 'no fixed gear' and 'very poor rock, very poor pro,' so expect to sling a horn/block or build a hand-placed gear anchor and inspect (or replace) any tat you find rather than trust it blindly. Below that step, continue down the same broken class 2–3 ground back to Crystal Pass, then reverse the approach: down into Crystal Basin, over Constance Pass, and back down the Constance Pass Trail and Dosewallips Road to the washout trailhead. Loose rock and scree are a hazard the entire way off the summit block — this is classic crumbly Olympic metavolcanic rock — so keep parties tight and out of each other's fall line. There is no easier walk-off alternative; the class 4/low 5th step near the top is the only way through, whether downclimbed or rappelled.
patches.value: Descend by reversing the ascent line: scramble back down the East Ridge to the notch, downclimb or rappel the short rock step into the gully, then descend the discontinuous snow finger and the South Defile, watching for moats on both sides and for snow blocks that loosen as the day warms. Where the snow is firm and runs out safely, the lower couloir can be plunge-stepped or glissaded. Loose rock is a hazard the whole way off the summit, so keep the party close together and out of each other's fall line. From the broad couloir below the Thumb, walk back down Avalanche Canyon to Lake Constance, then descend the steep climbers' path and the closed Dosewallips Road to the washout.

patches.fact: Approach and camp: Lake Constance vs Dosewallips/Constance Pass/Crystal Pass
patches.expect: From the Dosewallips River Road washout (roughly 1 mile in from the old trailhead gate, elev. ~600 ft), the road has been closed to motor vehicles since a 2002 flood took out a ~300-ft section, but it remains open to foot and bicycle travel — most parties bike the flat, mostly-shaded roadbed to save time, working around the washout on a riverside bypass/use trail. Continue roughly 5.5 more miles of road-walking/biking to the old Dosewallips Campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end (about 6.5 mi and ~1,900 ft of cumulative gain from the gate). From there, pick up the Constance Pass Trail, which climbs steadily south/southwest through forest into subalpine parkland — accounts differ on exact trail mileage (roughly 5–8 additional miles depending on where the count starts), gaining to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft; the upper stretch is steep, open meadow and scree with the last reliable water at creek crossings below treeline and none above. From Constance Pass, leave the maintained trail and travel cross-country west, dropping into the head of Crystal Basin and climbing to Crystal Pass, the windswept notch on the Constance–Warrior massif dividing the Dosewallips (Crystal Basin) side from Avalanche Canyon. This stretch is talus, scree, and (early/mid-season) lingering snow and ice — the informal climbers' track fades near the pass, so careful route-finding is needed, and a rope/axe may be prudent on the snow remnant below the pass in early season. From Crystal Pass, descend into upper Avalanche Canyon — a barren, glacially carved basin between Mount Constance and Inner Constance — following an intermittent climbers' path through scree and talus, staying toward the right (north) side of the canyon past the distinctive 'Cat Ears' rock formation, then contour/climb toward the base of Inner Constance's northeast side. From there, a short step just above the pass leads into a rising traverse along the right side of the north ridge/crest on broken, blocky class 2–3 terrain with occasional class 4 (and low 5th class) moves where the crest steepens, working up to the summit. This Dosewallips/Crystal Pass approach (about 16 mi one-way, ~25.75 km) is considerably longer than the more commonly used Lake Constance approach into Avalanche Canyon (roughly 8 mi one-way) but avoids that trail's brutally steep, unmaintained, blowdown-choked lower section; expect a 2–3 day trip with a camp near Constance Pass or in upper Avalanche Canyon, and carry all the water you'll need above Constance Pass since only transient snowmelt is available higher up.
patches.value: From the Dosewallips River Road washout (~700 ft) — the road has been closed to motor vehicles since a 2002 flood but stays open to foot and bicycle travel — most parties bike the closed roadbed, getting around the washed-out section on a riverside bypass. Several miles up, an unsigned, unmaintained climbers' path leaves the roadbed and climbs very steeply up the narrow Constance Creek canyon: roughly 3,300 ft in about 2 miles, choked with blowdown in its lower part and with some hands-on scrambling higher up, past a small creekside bench near 3,100 ft, to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft, the usual camp (a wilderness permit is needed and the lake is a quota area). From the lake, head north into barren Avalanche Canyon on a faint, intermittent climbers' track and snow patches to the broad couloir below the Thumb, where the South Chute of Mount Constance and the South Gully of Inner Constance part ways. A much longer alternative follows the closed road to its old end, climbs the Constance Pass Trail and crosses Crystal Pass into the head of Avalanche Canyon; it avoids the Lake Constance path's steep lower section. Expect a 2–3 day trip either way.

results.evidence: The route page says that after the roof, a few pitches of class 4-low fifth lead to the false summit to the southwest, then the line rejoins the NW Buttress for a final low-angle pitch to the summit proper, and the descent goes down the north side. That supports pitch_detail/baseFinding over overview/descent_text/itinerary, but it is the only independent source found and the row's fields split 3 against 4, so no patch.
